strings.name: Mette Frederiksen
strings.role: Prime Minister of Denmark and Social Democratic Party leader
strings.summary: Mette Frederiksen entered Parliament after working with trade union youth, then served as employment minister and justice minister before becoming Denmark’s prime minister in 2019. She combines welfare-state policies and climate transition with stricter immigration policies, and has faced scrutiny over the pandemic response and mink cull. In 2026 she formed her third government, a four-party minority coalition, while remaining active in European security and support for Ukraine.
strings.coverageNote: Information checked through 18 November 2026. Recent activity is supported by a Copenhagen meeting on 10 November and reported remarks in Dublin on 12 November. Elections, coalition agreements and formal appointments are distinguished, as are political criticism and criminal judgments, and legal targets or aid commitments and completed outcomes.
strings.influence.rationale: As Denmark’s prime minister, she has shaped welfare, climate and European security policy and has influence in Nordic and transatlantic affairs.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birth and education
strings.facts.f1.value: Born on 19 November 1977 in Aalborg. She earned a bachelor’s degree in administration and social studies from Aalborg University in 2007 and a master’s in African studies from the University of Copenhagen in 2009. Both qualifications followed her first election to Parliament; they should not be placed entirely before her political career.
strings.facts.f2.label: Trade union and parliamentary beginnings
strings.facts.f2.value: She worked as a youth consultant for the Danish trade union confederation LO in 2000–2001. Initially elected for the Copenhagen area, she has represented North Jutland since 2019. She was deputy chair of the Social Democratic parliamentary group in 2005–2011.
strings.highlights.h1.title: Climate targets become law
strings.highlights.h1.text: During her first government, Parliament passed the Climate Act on 18 June 2020, setting a 2030 greenhouse-gas reduction target of 70% from 1990 levels. It became Act No. 965 of 26 June 2020. The measure had cross-party support; targets and duties to act are not proof that reductions have already been achieved or that she legislated alone.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Support for Ukraine and European security
strings.highlights.h2.text: Meeting students with Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Copenhagen on 10 November 2026, she reaffirmed support for Ukraine and linked its self-determination to European security. Security cooperation involves governments, parliaments and allies; political commitments do not by themselves establish that every equipment shipment has arrived or the war has ended.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Forms a third, four-party minority government
strings.timeline.t1.text: After the 24 March election, Social Democratic seats fell from 50 to 38. She announced a coalition agreement on 1 June and formally formed the government on 3 June with the Social Democrats, Green Left, Moderates and Social Liberal Party. This differs from the 2022 coalition that included Venstre, the Liberal Party.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Forms a coalition across the political centre
strings.timeline.t2.text: After the 1 November election, she formed her second government with the Liberal Party and the Moderates, replacing the first government’s single-party Social Democratic structure. The formal start differs from earlier December negotiations and announcements. This government continued until 3 June 2026.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Announces the nationwide mink cull
strings.timeline.t3.text: During the pandemic, the government announced that all farmed mink would be killed; the blanket order was subsequently found to lack legal authority. In 2022 a parliamentary committee majority strongly criticised her political responsibility but did not find established knowledge of the legal deficiency or intent to mislead, and did not support impeachment proceedings. This was not a comprehensive court acquittal.
strings.timeline.t4.title: First becomes prime minister
strings.timeline.t4.text: Following the 5 June parliamentary election, she formed a single-party Social Democratic minority government with parliamentary support from other left-wing parties. Supporting the government did not make all those parties members of the cabinet.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Becomes Social Democratic Party leader
strings.timeline.t5.text: She succeeded Helle Thorning-Schmidt unopposed at an extraordinary party congress. The Social Democrats had lost the premiership; her party leadership began before her prime ministerial tenure in 2019.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Moves to the justice ministry
strings.timeline.t6.text: A reshuffle in Thorning-Schmidt’s government moved her from employment to justice, where she served until 28 June 2015. That ministerial role is distinct from her later leadership of the government.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Becomes employment minister
strings.timeline.t7.text: She began her ministerial career in Thorning-Schmidt’s government, overseeing employment until 10 October 2014. She had already been an MP and deputy chair of her party’s parliamentary group.
strings.timeline.t8.title: First enters the Danish Parliament
strings.timeline.t8.text: Elected for the Social Democrats in the Copenhagen County constituency, she began her national parliamentary career. Later constituency changes do not represent repeated first entries to Parliament; she was not yet prime minister.
